en.title: The kitchen and the dining room
en.summary: The things in the kitchen and at the table, and how to ask for them politely.

paragraphs: Dinner is almost ready. Anna asks her brother Ben to help her lay the table.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.text: Ben, can you set the table, please?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Of course. Where are the plates?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.text: They are in the cupboard next to the fridge.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.text: They are in the drawer under the sink.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Got them. Do we need glasses too?

paragraphs: **1. Can you...? asks for help politely.** Can is a modal verb, so the main verb stays in its base form. Add please to be polite. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

blocks.html:
RequestReply
Can you set the table, please?Of course.
Can you pass the salt?Sure, here you are.

paragraphs: **2. Countable nouns have a plural.** Most plurals add -s: plate, plates; fork, forks. Some change: knife becomes knives. Use a number or some before them. See Introduction to Grammar: Substantives (nouns).

items: **Lay the table** and **set the table** mean the same thing.
The fridge is short for refrigerator. The word cooker means the stove in British English.
Cutlery means knives, forks and spoons together. It has no plural form.

paragraphs: In many British families the evening meal is eaten at a table, but it is also common to eat in front of the television. Sunday lunch is usually the biggest meal of the week.
